extracted.intended_audience: book designers, printers, typographers, librarians, bibliophiles, and publishers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing, printing, and producing books so that their material form (size, paper, type, ink, illustrations, binding) fits the book's content and serves legibility, durability, and aesthetic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling elements: size, paper, and type
rubrics_metrics.description: Size, paper, and type are the few controlling elements of a book; each, if decided upon first, determines the character of the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention of sizes (folio, quarto, octavo, etc.) calls up an ideal book for each dimension; the series of sizes is associated with decreasing paper thickness and type size. The proportions of the page, surface of the paper, and cut of the type will vary according to the chosen size and thus shape the all other design choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper quality (body, surface, tint, durability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper is the printing material par excellence; its three elements—body, surface, and tint—must all be considered and may determine book size or character of the type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer paper that is opaque and tough yet thin enough to make books compact—more akin to vellum than coarse parchment. Smooth surfaces can be beautiful (e.g., Baskerville) but should not be shiny. Paper should also be durable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type aims: legibility, beauty, and compactness (in that order)
rubrics_metrics.description: Type design should prioritize legibility first, then beauty, then compactness, though these aims may conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hair-lines, fussiness, and ugliness in type (William Morris's counsel). For children's books and newspapers legibility must have the right of way. If compactness is desired (e.g., newspapers), condense the style of writing rather than compressing the typeface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ink: color, tint, and richness
rubrics_metrics.description: Ink affects legibility and durability—generally it should be a rich black; color only for ornaments and used sparingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some earlier print is brown or gray, but the booklover demands black ink except in ornamentation. The best combination for the eye is said to be bluish-tinted ink on buff-tinted paper (practically untried). Use color only sparingly and with skill in decorative elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrations must harmonize with type and book
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations introduced in connection with type must harmonize with the relatively heavy lines of type; many illustration processes conflict with type and need special placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early black-line engravings harmonize. Processes from copper-plate to half-tone often conflict and should be placed where they are not seen adjacent to type (e.g., at the end of the book) or be covered with opaque tissue so that either the picture or the facing type-page will be seen alone. Pictures should 'belong to the book' and not merely be thrust into it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binding construction and functionality (sewing, lie-open, internal structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The binding is the book's clothing and protection; internal construction (sewing) is fundamental, and a well-bound book should lie open well—binding must serve the reader as well as the collector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sewing is 'the first element in time and importance.' The visible cover is only the jacket of the true cover; focus on internal integrity (sewing, boards, joints) so the book opens and reads well. Extravagant external ornamentation should not compromise functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness of design to content (form corresponds to substance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fitness means the material form of the book shall correspond to its spiritual substance—neither too fine nor too mean—and produce a commensurate esthetic impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designer must understand the book's 'soul' and select the most characteristic quality to express. Avoid 'millinery'—design merely to bait buyers—and beware of overreaching (e.g., making a trivial work look epic) or mismatching (e.g., bulky format for delicate writing). Reflect the artist's joy where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series design: coherent, general qualities across multiple works
rubrics_metrics.description: When designing a series, the designer must seize upon more general and less salient characteristics that run through the authors' works to create consistent, appropriate design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose elements that express common qualities (sweetness, grace, dignity, learning) across the series. Avoid treating very different works with the same inappropriate format (e.g., making a handy-volume Gibbon or a folio Lamb).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate size and format for function and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Select book size and thickness appropriate to the work’s purpose—portable pocket editions for travel, small delicate formats for certain literature, larger formats where necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically small sizes (Aldus, Elzevir) are often favored for portability and economy. Avoid needlessly bulky sizes for works that call for intimacy or portability; thickness, height, and width all contribute to the esthetic impression (e.g., plump Elzevirs vs. thin Alduses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Page proportions, margins, and surface choices
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportions of the page, the surface of the paper, and margins influence legibility and the book’s esthetic effect and should be chosen to suit the type and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page proportions vary with size and determine the cut of type and surface choices. Historical pages (Aldus) and treatments of capitals, catchwords, and spacing offer models; small differences in thickness and style materially affect esthetic outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing as interpretation: duty to meaning then esthetics
rubrics_metrics.description: The printer's first duty is to the meaning of the author and his second to esthetics; printing should help interpret and make the author's meaning evident to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use typographic resources (consistent letterforms, spacing, punctuation emphasis, indentation, leading) to make meaning leap to the eye; treat punctuation and paragraphing as enforceable visual cues rather than minor details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic clarity to enable rapid reading and reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Print should enable quicker, clearer reading than manuscript by virtue of condensation and mechanical sameness; typographic distinctions should guide the eye in reference works and dictionaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design pages so the eye can sweep and locate passages rapidly—clear contrasts of type, effective abbreviations and layout in reference works, and use of leading/indentation to show structure. Where typewriting is used, remember it is a by-product of typography and lacks some of its condensation and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic aids for poetry and long lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry benefits from typographic aids (indentation, leading, accents, pauses) to indicate inflection, caesura, and line construction; modern free meter needs more assistance to the reader's eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printers should not shy from employing printed accents or marks to indicate intended pauses or stresses (examples: asterisks for caesura). Indentation and leading can mediate rhythm and form; the printer should consider additional guide-posts analogous to music notation where useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between compactness and legibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Compactness of a book (smaller format or denser type) must not come at undue cost to legibility; one should prefer condensing prose style over compromising type forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For works that must be compact (e.g., pocket editions or newspapers) consider reducing text length or style rather than shrinking or tightening type to the point of reduced legibility. Compact type trade-offs should be carefully weighed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use color and ornamentation sparingly and skillfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Color and decorative ornamentation can enhance a book but should be used sparingly and only with great skill if they are to win a booklover's favor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gratuitous or clashing ornamentation; color should be subordinate and harmonize with type and paper. Excessive decoration for marketing ('millinery') is discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability and reasonable cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Properly made books should be durable and need not be extremely costly; very high price often indicates small edition, extravagant binding, or marketplace mispricing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support printers and publishers who produce worthy, well-made books; value workmanship (durability, good materials, sound sewing) over ornament or high retail price. Good design and materials can be achieved without prohibitive cost.
